Releases happen in two steps: upload, then switch.

1. **Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each JS bundle, stylesheet, image, and other asset in the release gets a name unique to that build (for example, `app.3f9c2a.js`). Nothing existing is overwritten, so the live site is unaffected while the upload runs.

2. **Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest tells the browser which asset files make up the site. Once it points at the new names, every browser that loads it gets the new release.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is what makes a release visible. If we switched first, browsers would immediately request files that don't exist yet and the page would break until the upload finished. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references is already in place when the switch happens. The release becomes a single cutover with no window where the site points at missing files.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still holds references to the old file names. It may fetch those files later, for example when lazy-loading a route, loading a deferred script, or pulling an image further down the page. If the old files were gone, those requests would fail and that user's page would break mid-session. Keeping the old assets lets every browser finish with the release it started on. Versioned names make this possible, because old and new files never share a name and can coexist.

Our static-site releases happen in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names. The order matters, and so does leaving the old assets in place.

**Why the upload comes before the switch:** The manifest tells browsers which asset files to load. If we switched it first, it would point at files that don't exist yet, and any browser that fetched it during that window would get 404s for scripts, styles or images, leaving a broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names is already in place the moment the manifest goes live. Because the names are versioned, the uploads don't overwrite anything the current site uses, so the live site stays intact during the upload.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. A user with the site open, or a browser holding a cached copy of the old manifest, will keep requesting the old asset names, sometimes well after the release, for example when lazy-loading a route or chunk. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit missing files and broken pages until they reloaded. Keeping the old assets lets every client finish using whichever version it started with, while new visitors get the new version.

In short, each manifest only ever points at files that exist, from the moment it's published until the last browser using it is done.

Our static-site releases happen in two steps: first we upload the new assets, then we switch the manifest to point at them.

**Upload.** Every new asset (JavaScript, CSS, images) is uploaded under a versioned name, usually one that includes a content hash, such as `app.3f9c1a.js`. Because each version gets a new name, an upload never overwrites a file that a live page might be using.

**Switch.** Once every new asset is in place, we update the manifest to reference the new names. A browser that loads the manifest after the switch gets the new release.

**Why the upload comes first.** As soon as the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the files it names. If the manifest were switched first, or partway through the upload, those requests would hit files that don't exist yet. Users would see 404s and broken pages until the upload finished. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest is already available, so the switch takes effect for users in one step.

**Why we keep the old assets.** Some browsers loaded the previous manifest before the switch and may not have fetched every file it references yet. Examples include an open tab that lazy-loads a code chunk later, or a page whose manifest was served from a cache. Those browsers still request the old names. If we deleted the old assets at release time, those requests would fail, and users with the site already open would break partway through a session. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with. Rollback is also simple: point the manifest back at the previous names, and those files are still there.

A release has two steps: upload the new assets, then switch the manifest to point at them. The manifest is what tells a browser which asset files to load, so changing it is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first**

Each asset is uploaded under a new versioned name, so the upload doesn't overwrite any file that's currently being served. Until the manifest changes, nothing references the new files and users see no difference. That makes the upload safe to do at any pace.

If we switched the manifest first, browsers would immediately start requesting files that don't exist yet. They'd get 404s for scripts, styles or images, and pages would break until the upload finished. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names is already in place the instant a browser can see that manifest. The switch is the only step users can observe, and it moves them from one complete set of assets to another.

**Why we keep the old assets**

Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one. A page that loaded before the switch keeps using the old manifest and may still request old assets afterwards. For example, it might lazily load a script chunk, image or font when the user navigates. Browsers and caches may also keep serving the old manifest for a while after the switch. If we deleted the old files, those requests would fail and the user's page would break mid-session.

Keeping the old assets lets those clients finish on the version they started with, while new page loads pick up the new manifest. It also makes rollback simple: point the manifest back at the previous names, and everything it references is still there.

Old assets can only be removed once no client could still be holding a manifest that references them. That means waiting longer than the manifest can stay cached plus a typical session length.
